# Service interactions under latency and load constraints

## Start with one representative question

[S04-Q011](#S04-Q011)

<p>For a service interaction, how would you choose between synchronous REST/gRPC and asynchronous messaging? Explain what the choice means for the caller and for failure handling.</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Choose a service interaction whose response and overload behavior meet an explicit user contract.</p>

<ul>
<li>Trace waiting, completion and failure across a synchronous or asynchronous interaction.</li>
<li>Locate the resource that limits useful horizontal scaling.</li>
<li>Compare communication choices using latency, overload and recovery requirements.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

- [Dependency direction and service ownership](architecture-boundaries.md)

<p>First follow how work enters a system, is distributed and reaches a constrained dependency. Then compare communication styles against that flow: the caller&#x27;s waiting contract and the system&#x27;s ability to absorb or reject work must be considered together.</p>

<a id="S04-Q014"></a>

### S04-Q014 · Mechanism

<p>How do horizontal scaling, load balancing, backpressure and load shedding address increasing traffic? Explain their roles when a downstream resource is already saturated.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q014](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q014)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q014](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q014)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain horizontal scaling, load balancing, backpressure and load shedding.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Horizontal scaling adds replicas; the question asks what happens to work as it enters and moves through the system. Define overload behavior rather than assuming more workers solve every bottleneck.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Trace capacity and overload behavior across a service interaction.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the arrival pattern, shared resource limits and acceptable rejection or delay; use proposed measurements, not invented capacity figures.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Locate the limiting resource and explain how incoming work affects it.</li>
<li>Compare delay, rejection and added replicas against user and recovery constraints.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Adding application replicas while ignoring the saturated shared dependency.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you determine whether traffic should wait or be rejected?</li>
<li>Which measurement would show that scaling added useful capacity?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q011"></a>

### S04-Q011 · Trade-offs

<p>For a service interaction, how would you choose between synchronous REST/gRPC and asynchronous messaging? Explain what the choice means for the caller and for failure handling.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q011](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q011)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q011](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q011)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare synchronous REST/gRPC communication with asynchronous messaging.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare waiting for a response with arranging work whose result may arrive later. Clarify which parts concern interaction timing and which concern protocol.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose a communication style from response and reliability requirements.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State when the caller needs an outcome, acceptable delay and delivery requirements; verify provider-specific guarantees separately.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Trace response ownership and failure propagation for both options.</li>
<li>Give a requirement that changes the preferred choice and a validation plan.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming asynchronous messaging removes failures or that REST alone specifies the timing contract.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What should the caller do if the outcome is still unknown?</li>
<li>How would you compare latency and operational cost for the two designs?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A checkout API calls an inventory service while a SQL Server dependency is saturated. Compare a synchronous interaction with an asynchronous alternative. Define the caller-visible outcome, capacity hypothesis, overload behavior and measurements that would validate the choice without assuming more replicas solve the shared bottleneck.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Distinguishes waiting for a result from receiving a result later and recognizes a bottleneck.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Connects interaction choice to business completion, failure propagation and measured overload behavior.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A preferred protocol without a response contract, failure trace or capacity measurement is not yet a defended design.</p>
